title: Six Flags acquires fan-favourite ArieForce One coaster
summary:
Six Flags has acquired ArieForce One, the 15-story steel roller coaster that opened at Fun Spot America Atlanta in 2023.

Built by Rocky Mountain Construction, the coaster closed last month when Fun Spot America Atlanta in Fayetteville, Georgia, shut down.

The ride became popular with enthusiasts for its combination of speed, airtime and inversions, building a following among visitors from across the US and overseas.

View this post on Instagram
A post shared by FPV From A Different POV (@blastrfpv)

According to a press release, Six Flags will introduce the attraction at one of its parks during the 2028-2029 operating seasons. The coaster's future home remains under wraps.

Six Flags described ArieForce One as "one of the most acclaimed coaster experiences of the modern era", adding that it will "retain the classic ArieForce One name, honouring the coaster’s history and preserving the identity that helped make it a fan favourite".

"From the moment ArieForce One closed, we knew how much this coaster meant to the enthusiast community and to guests who travelled from around the world to experience it," said Mark Pauls, chief operating officer of Six Flags.

He added: "This is a ride that consistently generated excitement, acclaim and passionate fan support. We are thrilled to preserve its legacy, invest in its future and bring this extraordinary attraction to a new generation of guests.

"This acquisition represents our commitment to delivering world-class thrills and creating unforgettable experiences across the Six Flags portfolio."

Coaster's future home remains under wraps

The coaster was named after Fun Spot America founder John Arie Sr and represented a major investment by the family-owned company.

"When we built ArieForce One, we wanted to create something truly special. Something that would put Fun Spot America on the map with coaster enthusiasts and families around the world and create memories that would last a lifetime," said John Arie Jr, CEO of Fun Spot America.

"Seeing ArieForce One preserved and finding a new home with Six Flags means a great deal to me and my family. Its story isn't ending, it's beginning a new chapter, and we are excited that future generations will get to experience ArieForce One."

title: Studio Ghibli theme park: everything you need to know
summary:
Studio Ghibli, the animation house behind classics including My Neighbor Totoro and Princess Mononoke, announced plans for Ghibli Park in 2017. The theme park, which opened in November 2022, also features areas inspired by Kiki's Delivery Service, Spirited Away and Castle in the Sky.

Located in the Expo 2005 Aichi Commemorative Park, Ghibli Park was projected to generate an annual economic impact of approximately $324 million before opening. It is expected to welcome approximately 1.8 million visitors annually, with all five themed areas now open.

Keep reading for everything you need to know about the Studio Ghibli theme park, including attractions, inspiration, location and cost.

When did the anime theme park open?

The Studio Ghibli theme park opened in November 2022. Guests could visit three of the five themed lands – Ghibli's Grand Warehouse, Dondoko Forest and Hill of Youth. Aichi's governor Hideaki Ōmura and Studio Ghibli co-founder Hayao Miyazaki's son Goro Miyazaki welcomed the venue's first visitors.

Mononoke Village opened in November 2023 and was followed by Valley of Witches in March 2024.

The Kashira, the three green rolling heads from Spirited Away, are on display in Ghibli's Grand WarehouseGhibli Park

At a press event before the launch, Ōmura said Ghibli Park had taken "five years and five months" to complete (via Lifestyle Asia ). Miyazaki said the destination was designed before his father's retirement. "We didn't want people to forget Ghibli's works," he said. "But we were betrayed again. He's making a feature film now!"

Ghibli Park was initially set to open in 2020. It was revealed in July 2020 that the attraction had resumed construction following a temporary suspension. "We are still on track and are planning to open the park in fall 2022," Ōmura confirmed at the time.

Ghibli Park is located in Nagakute, close to Nagoya, the capital of Japan's Aichi PrefectureGhibli Park

Building work on Ghibli Park started in early 2020. Then, it paused temporarily in response to the pandemic. Work soon resumed and started on Hill of Youth, Ghibli's Grand Warehouse and Dondoko Forest.

Studio Ghibli held a groundbreaking ceremony in the summer of 2020. Its chairman, Kiyofumi Nakajima, was in attendance. At the event, Ōmura said: "The 2005 Expo's theme of 'love' has also been portrayed in Studio Ghibli's films consistently, so we can inherit that philosophy. We aim to make the facility a world-class park and hope many people will visit here."

Where is the Studio Ghibli theme park located?

The Studio Ghibli theme park can be found on 7.1 hectares of land within the former site of the 2005 World Expo. It is located in Nagakute, close to Nagoya, the capital of Japan's Aichi Prefecture.

A large-scale Yubaba is located in Ghibli's Grand Warehouse, inside the Director's Room exhibit, a recreation of Yubaba's office from Spirited AwayGhibli Park

The land already featured a replica of Satsuki and Mei's house from the Studio Ghibli film My Neighbor Totoro, created for the World Expo. Developers maintained the house for the new park.

What anime attractions feature at Ghibli Park?

Unlike theme parks like Tokyo Disneyland, Tokyo DisneySea and Universal Studios Japan, Ghibli Park has no major thrill rides or roller coasters, but Valley of Witches includes several small amusement rides. Ahead of the park's debut, Studio Ghibli launched an official website. "Ghibli Park is a park that represents the world of Studio Ghibli," it said. "There are no big attractions or rides in Ghibli Park. Take a stroll, feel the wind, and discover the wonders."

Ghibli's Grand Warehouse is just one of five themed lands at Ghibli Park in JapanGhibli Park

As mentioned above, the Studio Ghibli theme park is divided into five themed lands, which are: Ghibli's Grand Warehouse, Dondoko Forest, Mononoke Village, Hill of Youth, and Valley of Witches.

Themed lands

Hill of Youth is located at the park's entrance and features the World Emporium, one of the locations from Whisper of the Heart and the Cat Bureau from The Cat Returns. Also in this area is a giant elevator tower inspired by the late 19th-century sci-fi architecture seen in Castle in the Sky and Howl's Moving Castle.

Children's Town recreates a miniature Higashi-Koganei Station neighbourhood as a children’s play area inside Ghibli's Grand WarehouseGhibli Park

Ghibli's Grand Warehouse is "a large warehouse full of Ghibli secrets", home to a small cinema, playgrounds, shops, cafés and immersive exhibits.

At Dondoko Forest, visitors can "enter the world of My Neighbor Totoro at Satsuki and Mei's house". The surrounding area serves as the rural landscape from the film.

Valley of Witches features Ghibli Park’s first amusement-style rides, including a carousel and aerial Flying Machine rideGhibli Park

Mononoke Village is a Princess Mononoke -style area in Ghibli Park. It is inspired by the film's setting of Irontown (Tatara), protected by a lake and high walls. It houses a sculpture of a Tatarigami spirit monster, the boar god Lord Okkoto and more mystical creatures. The land transports visitors back to the Muromachi period (1336 - 1573) when the film is set.

At Tatara-ba in Mononoke Village, visitors can grind roasted soybeans into fresh kinako on a traditional stone mill before enjoying it with warabi-mochi. The seasonal workshop is typically held during the warmer months, replacing the charcoal-grilled gohei-mochi experience.

Valley of Witches takes inspiration from the wastelands in Kiki's Delivery Service and Howl's Moving Castle. The area contains a life-size Howl's Moving Castle, the witch's house from Earwig and the Witch, and Ghibli Park's first amusement park-style rides, like a merry-go-round and an aerial carousel ride.

Additionally, Valley of Witches includes the bakery home of Kiki and her black cat Jiji from Kiki's Delivery Service, the Soratobu Oven restaurant, a hot dog stand called the Hot Tin Roof, and a shop named 13 Witches.

On 7 August, 2026, Aichi Prefecture announced plans for a new indoor Ghibli Park area inspired by Hayao Miyazaki's 1984 film Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind. The proposed facility would be the park's second fully indoor area after Ghibli's Grand Warehouse, with details and an opening date yet to be announced.

Large-scale Howl's Moving Castle

As above, Valley of Witches includes a large-scale recreation of Howl's Moving Castle. The attraction at Ghibli Park doesn't actually move, and it is slightly smaller than the version seen in the 2004 film.

Valley of Witches features a large-scale recreation of Howl’s Moving Castle, allowing visitors to explore its detailed interior spacesGhibli Park

My Neighbor Totoro -themed playground

Concept art and information about the My Neighbor Totoro -themed playground at Ghibli's Grand Warehouse were released in the summer of 2021. The playground includes a replica of Satsuki and Mei's house, a giant camphor tree, and a redesigned Catbus.

Ghibli's Grand Warehouse is an indoor area of the park with a small cinema, shops, cafés and immersive exhibits. Cinema Orion screens 10 short animation films produced by Studio Ghibli. Until now, these have only been shown at the Ghibli Museum in Mitaka.

Guests can travel around the Studio Ghibli theme park using Catbus electric vehiclesGhibli Park

Highlights at Ghibli's Grand Warehouse also include the train from Spirited Away, where guests can sit next to No-Face. Additionally, this land boasts an expanded version of the Ghibli Museum's 'Drawing Eating' exhibition.

Castle in the Sky -style entrance

Ghibli Park also has a Castle in the Sky -style elevator tower entrance, which launched to the public before the theme park. Studio Ghibli said it is "based on the fantasy science world at the end of the 19th century, which became the model of the world of Castle in the Sky."

A large model of the Savoia S-21 seaplane from Porco Rosso went on display at Rotunda Kazegaoka in November 2025. Located at Ghibli Park's main entrance, the café and shop can be visited without a Ghibli Park ticket.

Ghibli Park features a Castle in the Sky-inspired elevator tower entrance, welcoming visitors to the parkGhibli Park

Getting around Ghibli Park

Guests can now travel around the Studio Ghibli theme park using Catbus electric vehicles. In March 2024, Ghibli Park debuted a fleet of eco-friendly vehicles inspired by the Catbus in My Neighbor Totoro. Officially called APM Catbus, the vehicles look and feel like the Catbus from the film, with a rounded appearance and furry seats.

Six Catbus vehicles transport up to six passengers each, providing rides around Ghibli ParkGhibli Park

The low-speed electric vehicles developed by Toyota, originally for the Tokyo Olympics, are based on the manufacturer's APM (Accessible People Mover). Operated by software company Monet Technologies, six Catbus vehicles can carry six passengers at a time across the park. The APM Catbus offers 10-minute trips between the Mononoke Village and Dondoko Forest areas through an inaccessible forest.

The new buses are 3.9 metres long, 1.6 metres wide, and 2 metres high. They can travel at a top speed of 19 km/h and can seat six people, including the driver. The front row contains the driver's seat, and there are three seats in the second row and two in the third.

The Ghibli Park vehicles recreate the Catbus with rounded designs, soft furry seats, and details inspired by the filmGhibli Park

Catbuses run from 9.30 am until 5.30 pm on weekdays and from 8.30 am until 5.30 pm on weekends and public holidays. Guests can buy tickets for a ride on a Catbus at special vending machines. Only one-way tickets are available, as opposed to round-trip tickets. These cost 1,000 yen ($6) for adults and 500 yen ($3) for children.

Museum exhibit with items from Ghibli Park

Before Studio Ghibli's theme park opened, the Aichi Prefectural Museum of Art showcased items from the attraction. The themed exhibit was a final preview of some of the park's contents before they made their way to Ghibli's Grand Warehouse. It also explored Studio Ghibli's 35-year history and displayed previously unreleased material.

The World of Arrietty recreates the Borrowers’ tiny world inside Ghibli’s Grand Warehouse through oversized household objectsGhibli Park

In addition, the exhibit brought back content shown in earlier Studio Ghibli exhibits. The first of these ran in 2015 at Moricoro Park before touring Japan and Seoul. The previous exhibits displayed memorabilia such as artwork, memos, and film posters.

Ghibli Park's colourful 'Cattrain' trailer

Before the opening, the new Studio Ghibli theme park released a colourful trailer directed and animated by Hayao Miyazaki. The trailer features a My Neighbor Totoro -style ' Cattrain', similar to the film's Catbus.

The video, which you can see above, features several characters from Studio Ghibli's films. These include Totoro and Mei from My Neighbor Totoro and the Radish Spirit and No-Face in Spirited Away.

The trailer is an adaptation of an animated video by Miyazaki for the launch of the Ghibli Museum in Mitaka, Japan, in 2001. It offers music by Studio Ghibli composer Joe Hisaishi and narration by Toshio Suzuki, co-founder and former president of the animation company.

Howl's Moving Castle -style promo video

Ghibli Park released an animated video inspired by Howl's Moving Castle before the launch of the Valley of Witches area.

Miyazaki created the storyboards for the short video, while Howl's Moving Castle animation director Akihiko Yamashita provided direction and original drawings. Noboru Yoshida, the art director of Howl's Moving Castle, created the new video.

Immersing visitors in nature

Ghibli Park is an eco-friendly place. Studio Ghibli will not cut down any trees to make room for future attractions. During construction, the team enhanced and preserved any natural areas.

Mononoke Village at Ghibli Park features towering boar statues inspired by the creatures and themes of Princess Mononoke Ghibli Park

Studio Ghibli's theme park celebrates the natural beauty that inspired the company's lush animation. Nature trails feature statues of spiders, boars, and other Ghibli characters, and there are plenty of natural spaces, like the settings of many Ghibli films.

Instead of thrill rides and coasters, Ghibli Park focuses on immersing visitors in the worlds of Studio Ghibli. The park even limits daily attendance within each of its themed lands to improve the guest experience and protect the park and its environment.

Tickets to the Studio Ghibli theme park

The current ticket system focuses on the type of pass you purchase rather than whether you are a domestic or overseas visitor. International guests book through a different sales channel.

The two main ticket options are:

Ghibli Park O-Sanpo Day Pass Premium

Includes admission to all five areas of Ghibli Park, all eligible buildings and attractions, shops, restaurants, and the amusement rides in Valley of Witches.

Ghibli Park O-Sanpo Day Pass Standard

Includes admission to Ghibli's Grand Warehouse, Valley of Witches and Mononoke Village. It also includes access to shops, restaurants and rides within those areas, but does not include entry to Hill of Youth, Dondoko Forest or certain buildings in Valley of Witches.

Standard Pass holders can purchase same-day tickets for selected buildings in Valley of Witches, including Howl's Castle, Okino Residence and The House of Witches, subject to availability. Admission to Hill of Youth and Dondoko Forest is only available with the Premium Pass.

Regardless of your pass type, you must select a one-hour timed entry slot for Ghibli's Grand Warehouse. Premium Pass holders may re-enter all areas, although re-entry to Ghibli's Grand Warehouse is only permitted after 3:00 p.m.

Highlights at Ghibli's Grand Warehouse also include the train from Spirited Away, where guests can sit next to No-FaceGhibli Park

Ticket prices

Ghibli Park O-Sanpo Day Pass Premium

Adults: 7,300 yen ($45) (weekdays) / 7,800 yen ($48) (weekends and holidays)

Children (ages 4–12): 3,650 yen ($22) / 3,900 yen ($24)

This all-access pass includes admission to all five areas, every eligible building, shops, restaurants and rides.

Ghibli Park O-Sanpo Day Pass Standard

Adults: 3,300 yen ($20) (weekdays) / 3,800 yen ($23) (weekends and holidays)

Children (ages 4–12): 1,650 yen ($10) / 1,900 yen ($12)

This pass includes admission to Ghibli's Grand Warehouse, Valley of Witches and Mononoke Village. Entry to Hill of Youth and Dondoko Forest is not included. Visitors can also purchase same-day tickets for selected Valley of Witches buildings, subject to availability.

Same-day building ticket prices are:

Okino Residence: 400 yen ($2) for adults, 200 yen ($1) for children

Howl's Castle: 1,000 yen ($6) for adults, 500 yen ($3) for children

The House of Witches: 400 yen ($2) for adults, 200 yen ($1) for children

Children aged 3 and under receive free admission.

International visitors can purchase tickets through the English Lawson Ticket website or Klook.

Tickets go on sale on the 10th of each month, two months in advance, at 2pm Japan Standard Time.

In comparison, tickets to Tokyo Disneyland and Universal Studios Japan cost up to $80 per person. However, Ghibli Park is a smaller venue without big attractions and rides.

title: Valo Motion launches new mixed-reality attraction, ValoBoard
summary:
Valo Motion, a pioneer in combining interactive technology with physical activities, introduces its second new product in 2026: ValoBoard. This multiplayer mixed-reality board attraction aims to make the excitement of board sports more accessible.

ValoBoard, the fifth addition to the Valo Motion product line, is also the first designed around a physical controller. It will make its debut at IAAPA Expo Europe 2026 at ExCeL London.

Guests step onto a tilt board, and ValoVision, Valo Motion’s exclusive full-body tracking system, immerses them in the game world displayed on the screens ahead. They shift their weight to steer, lean to aim, and jump to dodge obstacles, with their movements recorded instantly.

Making board sports more accessible

“Board sports have captured people’s imagination for decades, but experiencing that rush is often out of reach," says Dr Raine Kajastila, CEO of Valo Motion.

"You need a mountain, an ocean, or years of learning to master them. ValoBoard removes those barriers, making the excitement of board sports accessible to a much wider audience. It takes balance and core strength and turns them into a fun, multiplayer game experience.

"For our operators, ValoBoard opens up an exciting new category of fantasy board sports. It delivers multiplayer fun on a compact footprint, appeals to a broad range of guests, and runs without staff. We are proud to show it for the first time at IAAPA Expo Europe this year, on Valo Motion’s 10th anniversary."

Key product details for operators include a footprint of 15 square metres (161 square feet) under a standard 2.7 metre (8 foot 11) ceiling, requiring no structural modifications or special flooring. The system supports 2- to 3-minute sessions and accommodates 70 to 74 riders per hour with gated admission using Rush Hour mode.

It is operated unmanned, eliminating the need for wearables, headsets, or guest onboarding, and requires no maintenance. Supported business models include gated admission and pay-to-play, with remote management via Operations Hub, Valo Motion's cloud platform for scheduling, branding, and performance monitoring.

Each ride session ends with a QR code that guests can scan to receive a branded video of their ride, encouraging organic social sharing and helping the operator acquire new customers.

Three original games

ValoBoard is suitable for guests aged 6 and up and especially appeals to teenagers and young adults who often compare attractions to the games they already enjoy at home. The three launch games are designed to meet these expectations: engaging mixed-reality experiences that are easy to learn but challenging to master.

A still from Sunset Skaters, one of three new games launching with ValoBoard

Sunset Skaters is a fast-paced skating race across three lanes. Trickpunk Snowboarding offers a mountain sandbox where each rider can choose their own path down. Spinblades is a two-player head-to-head battle on a floating platform.

All three games attract cautious first-time players, competitive groups, and returning guests aiming for higher scores.

Valo Motion is showcasing ValoBoard and Groundfall, launched earlier in 2026, at booth #S2502 at ExCeL London from 22 - 24 September.

Kajastila will introduce the new products and reflect on the company’s first decade during a press conference at the booth on Tuesday 22 September 22, at 3:20 p.m. The Valo Motion team will be available throughout the event to provide demos, and all visitors are welcome to try out the new offerings.

title: Lee Cowie, CEO of accesso, on AI and the future of the attractions industry
summary:
In May, Lee Cowie was named the new CEO of accesso following an 18-month tenure as COO. He brings a vision for the future informed by his experiences working within four different industries as they reached their technological turning points.

Today, he argues, technology is no longer simply a support function but is fundamental to the success of attractions in a rapidly changing landscape.


  • Technology as a transformational force. Cowie emphasises that technology, particularly AI, is fundamentally reshaping the attractions industry, requiring operators to view digital experiences as equally important to physical ones.
  • Empathy and operational context. Drawing from his background as an operator, Cowie highlights empathy as a key differentiator, providing a deep understanding of the unique pressures and capital-intensive nature of visitor attractions.
  • The critical role of context in AI. He argues that generic AI is insufficient for the industry; successful deployment requires context, which accesso provides by integrating its 20 years of sector-specific knowledge with venue-proprietary data.
  • Operational backbone vs. insight. Cowie insists that operational platforms are "load-bearing"; insight is wasted without the ability to act on it rapidly, making robust, connected systems essential for business success.
  • Human-centric AI. Rather than replacing humans, Cowie believes AI should be used to automate mundane tasks, freeing up staff to focus on creating emotional connections and managing the guest experience—which remains the industry's most valuable use of human time.


As a leading technology provider for attractions worldwide, accesso is uniquely positioned to support attractions in this critical moment by leveraging its 20 years of sector-specific data to create actionable insights, ensuring venues can navigate complex operational challenges.

As Cowie takes the reins, he speaks to blooloop about the next steps for accesso, and advocates for a human-centric approach to AI.

​At the vanguard


Cowie has worked across four industries, each at a critical point at which technology reshaped the sector.

His first role at Aviva coincided with the dot-com boom and the rush to get online.

“That was the first time I really saw that tech can absolutely, fundamentally transform how an entire industry works,” he says.

“Then, I was fortunate enough to see that pattern repeat.”

Cowie moved into broadcast media just as the industry was being disrupted by Netflix, Amazon Prime, and BBC iPlayer, then to Nando's as F&B embraced new technologies.

Before joining accesso, he served as CTO at Merlin Entertainments and has deep operational experience in the sector.

“The same is playing out now in the attractions space.

“For the longest time in attractions, it was all about the physical experience, about the quality of being on site and present in that attraction.


“Now it's equally as important to consider the digital experience, the bit that gets you up to the attraction in the first place and then the bit that curates your experience.”

Across all four industries, he has seen that the companies that kept investing through disruption defined the era that followed. The ones that waited came out behind.

“If I've learned anything,” he adds, “it's to assume that everything will change very rapidly.”

​Operational empathy


Many technology leaders have spent their careers on the vendor side. However, while at Merlin, Cowie was responsible for technology used by tens of millions of guests every year.

This operational background is echoed throughout the wider accesso team, giving the company a distinctive approach.

“It's been a very deliberate policy,” says Cowie. “Whether you're talking about our ski division, where most people have grown up and lived on the slopes and then have come to join us, or attractions and theme parks.

“I think the thing it gives us is empathy; a unique understanding that location-based entertainment and attractions operate differently from many other sectors.

“We know how critical timing is. It's the difference between hitting or missing a complete season. If you don't get your tech enabled, you've got to wait another 12 months for that to come around.”

The combination of deep knowledge and technical capabilities means the accesso team has an intricate understanding of context across roles, domains, systems, and attributes, and ultimately how these impact the visitor experience.


“Attractions are capital-intensive businesses and most of the spare cash goes into making the physical experience as good as it can be, which leaves breadcrumbs normally for technology.

"And operators are under unique pressures to service their guests.

“Because there is a lot of competition for people's time and attention now, it's critical that people deliver a really good experience in the moment. Otherwise they may lose that visitor forever.”

​Context is critical


AI, Cowie says, is set to be the key to delivering these experiences.

“I suspect it will change everything,” he says. “It gives venues capabilities that were beyond their means, beyond their reach even two years ago.”

However, this transformation depends on a sophisticated use of the technology that surpasses generic AI.

“ChatGPT is not going to give you the answers. It will give you an answer and express it very confidently, and you might be tempted to believe it. But it will actually be based on a set of really poor assumptions and will end up delivering you down the wrong track.

“The important thing about AI is to be able to feed it context.”


Last year, accesso acquired Dexibit, an industry analytics and intelligence platform that has analysed millions of visitor reviews across hundreds of attractions globally over a full decade.

It has used this as a platform to develop accesso Intelligence.

“This allows us to embed our 20 years of sector-specific knowledge into a platform that then feeds AI,” says Cowie.

“It changes AI from being a guessing machine to being something that can act on data that is only available to your venue. That is proprietary to you and can only be accessed by you.

“It changes from being guesswork to being a genuinely useful tool. And the deployment opportunities for that are endless. There is no part of an operation that will be unaffected by AI.”

​The Voice of the Visitor


Drawing from accesso Intelligence, the company has published The Voice of the Visitor 2026 Industry Benchmark Report.

This represents the largest AI-analysed body of visitor-attraction sentiment ever assembled and underscores Cowie’s belief that the sector is now experiencing its own inflection point.

“We covered two and a half million data points across a decade of guest feedback in 500 attractions, 37 countries,” says Cowie. “It was huge, and sobering to read.”


The sector, the report found, has not recovered from COVID-19. Rather, as the cost of living and expectations rise, disappointment is at its highest level since the pandemic.

Another key finding is that the difference between the best and worst attractions in the world lies in operations and technology, while staff friendliness remains constant.

“It is much harder for attractions to stand out from the crowd, and it is a very crowded marketplace,” says Cowie.

“Feedback across the board has been that guests expect much more. The bar is much higher for what counts as a good attraction or experience.

“And trust is fragile. It's easy to lose an advocate through a bad experience. Attractions will have to work much harder, and I think technology can help make that happen.

“A visitor is one person in a crowd of, say, 50,000 on any particular day. The trick will be to make that one person feel like they are alone on the attraction and deliver the experience they want.

“That's where technology will help deliver personalisation at scale.”

​Preparing for the AI era


So, as Cowie takes the helm of accesso, AI arrives in the sector at a particularly pressured, demanding, and technically consequential moment, and operators need their infrastructure to be ready. Yet knowing where to begin is half the battle.

“This is one of the great quandaries with AI,” says Cowie. “You’ve got the extreme viewpoint: what's the point of humans? That sounds like a horrible world to live in.

“I take a more optimistic view; I don't think AI will replace humans. I think it will augment them.

“We're a long way off from having conviction that everything AI tells us is true. So there'll always need to be a human in the loop.

“What will shift is our understanding of what people need to be.


“In the attraction space, I think we've got a huge opportunity. The most valuable use of human time at any attraction is to engage with other people. To visit guests, see how their day is going, and create an emotional connection.

“Humans excel at that. AI is rubbish at it.

“AI will free up people's time, so that attractions can think long and hard about where the human beings have most value. And I believe it will be in managing the guest experience.”

​Introducing agentic booking


Another key question that operators need to address is what happens to ecommerce when AI agents start booking tickets?

According to Edgar, Dunn and Company, AI agents are set to account for 37% of UK ticket sales by 2028.

“There's no real one definition of agentic commerce at the minute,” says Cowie. “It'll take some time before that forms a standard that everybody can adopt.

“But one of the great things an agent could do is learn your preferences and understanding, then search for experiences you might be interested in. And eventually, negotiate your ideal day with other people's agents.”

This is most likely to affect OTAs, travel agents, and content aggregators first, he adds.


“We'll see a cascade of impact as it transforms our industry, starting at the point closest to the consumer and then working down.”

To succeed in this new landscape, operators will need to understand new terminology.

“We've spent a decade talking about SEO or search engine optimisation. We're going to spend the next decade talking about GEO, generative engine optimisation.

“It's the same discipline, just with a different audience. It's something that we are watching very closely because it's a rapidly evolving space.”

​Insight to action


This rapid evolution fuels fears about the trustworthiness of AI.

“I don't think AI really gives you more risk; it will get you into trouble much more quickly than previous approaches would,” says Cowie, and heeds caution.

“It all comes down to good data governance, having the appropriate controls, making sure that your context window is PII-free (personally identifiable information).

“We've got an obligation to society and to individuals. We have an obligation to the legislation to treat people's data with the respect it deserves.

“We certainly build all our systems with that in mind. And venues will need to do the same.”


Establishing such tight data governance requires operators to refocus on their operational backbone. This, Cowie says, is the "load-bearing" part of a business that often gets pushed to the bottom of the pile but underpins AI adoption.

“If you follow the hyperbole that exists around AI, there’s a view that your entire business model is going to be broken; you've got to find something new. That's just not true.

“AI is currently awesome at surfacing insight if you give it good context. But insight alone is not useful unless you can actually act on it.”

“If you've uncovered a nugget, but you've got no way to actually do something about it, it's wasted.

“So having good operational platforms to act on insight in a timely manner is going to be increasingly important.”

​Building an integrated, powerful platform


Since Cowie first joined accesso as COO in 2025, the company has made three major moves.

In addition to launching accesso Intelligence, it has implemented a new payments strategy and is now integrating all of its technologies.

“The integration effort is about strengthening that operational backbone and making sure that our systems connect in the right way to support an AI world,” says Cowie.

“The accesso Intelligence platform is evolving at a phenomenal rate. And then the payments piece is really interesting.

“Payments is a complex world. There are so many intermediaries.

“It's as easy as pie to get your Apple Wallet out and tap on a device. But behind that, there are handoffs among your bank, credit card companies, intermediary processes, and eventually the venue's bank.

“Each of those wants to be paid. And so, as a consumer may not see the cost, the operator has to pay their bank, Visa card fees, other banks in the chain, and it adds up.


“With accessoPay, we take all that away from a venue, and we manage it on their behalf.

“We process 5 billion in payments on our platforms each year. Because of our scale, we can buy at wholesale prices. We can negotiate really good prices and pass those savings on to our customers.

“So, they get a simpler relationship. They've only got to manage us, and we'll also save them some money on the way. So, it's genuinely win-win.”

​Driving value


As a result, the accesso ecosystem can curate the visitor experience, from the digital journey to buy a ticket to the venue.

“We can manage queue times, the food and beverage counters, and the retail counters. We can do targeted marketing messages to individuals through mobile apps,” says Cowie.

“Then we can connect all of those data sources to the accesso Intelligence platform, which allows an operator to understand what is going on in their venue.

“And this is sector-agnostic. It works brilliantly in ski. It works brilliantly in cultural attractions, zoos, aquariums, and theme parks.

“It's a pretty exciting vision, and I hope our customers can see the value.”


In addition to his aims for accesso, Cowie considers the shape of the sector as we approach a new decade.

“2030 is three and a half years away. Three and a half years ago, ChatGPT wasn't a thing.

“So anybody who can confidently predict what will happen in the next three and a half years is pretty foolish, I would say.

“But we have some sense of what will matter.

“AI is useless to you unless you give a good context. Operators that understand this sooner, and start aggregating their data and making it available to AI, will have a head start.

“The accesso Intelligence platform will help with that, as we augment it with our 20 years of context. But without context, AI will give you an answer that is worse than not having it at all.”

​Power in people


People, Cowie stresses, are key to success in the AI era.

“It is genuinely scary to people; the dystopian view some people have predicted is a horrible place to be. I'm certain it won't come to that.

“But I think it's important to acknowledge that, because ultimately humans are important,” says Cowie.


“They need to be treated as human beings, not just as people who turn a handle.

“Particularly in our sector. The reason attractions exist is to attract people and to give them an emotional and physical experience.

“The operators that succeed will not view AI as an opportunity to cut costs; that would be a dangerous path to go down.

“Those who succeed will realise that AI enables them to free people from the mundane and routine, and reinvest that time in the guest experience and in treating their visitors as human beings.”
